_meta.note: The 8 Jev rubric categories, one Jev `score` question each. This file is the source of truth (scripts/jev-gate is self-contained in CI). Instructions describe ONLY what to score and the level criteria — say NOTHING about confidence: confidence is the model's own axis (its certainty in the verdict), so the rubric must never instruct, calibrate, or nudge it; a low-confidence score already routes to human sign-off. Duplication was dropped 2026-09-19 — it needs cross-file context the per-file gate cannot supply, so its scores were never decidable.
_meta.scale: Every question is a Jev `score`. Levels run 0 (worst) to 4 (best). Higher always means healthier code, so the overall score is a plain mean.

code_smells.instructions: Rate this source code for Martin Fowler-style code smells such as long methods, large classes, feature envy, primitive obsession, data clumps, long parameter lists, speculative generality, and shotgun surgery. Also weight boolean/flag parameters that silently switch a function's behavior (control coupling) as a smell — a pattern that is easy to accumulate in TypeScript because optional booleans are cheap to add. Higher means fewer, less harmful smells.
criteria: Riddled with smells: bloated methods and classes, feature envy, primitive obsession, shotgun surgery, and/or flag-parameter control coupling throughout
Frequent smells that clearly hurt readability and make change unsafe
Some smells present but localized and low impact
Mostly clean; only minor, defensible smells remain
No meaningful code smells; cohesive and well factored

security.instructions: Rate this source code for security by EXPLOITABILITY, not by pattern-matching a checklist. For every candidate issue, ask: is there a concrete input an attacker or untrusted caller could supply that reaches a dangerous sink and causes real harm (auth bypass, code/command execution, cross-tenant data access, secret exposure, traversal outside an intended directory)? Weight heavily anything with a reachable, attacker-influenced path to a dangerous sink — including auth/access checks that fail OPEN (an error, missing token, or unknown case treated as authorized), command injection (untrusted data interpolated or spread into subprocess args or a shell:true call), path traversal (an unsanitized or unvalidated id/name joined into a filesystem path), unsafe deserialization, hardcoded secrets, injection (SQL/NoSQL/template), and broken or predictable cryptography reachable by an attacker (a non-CSPRNG source used for tokens/session ids/nonces, a fast general-purpose hash used for passwords, a hardcoded or reused IV/key). Also weight heavily error handling that leaks internal detail to an untrusted caller through the error itself — a stack trace, file path, internal identifier, or secret returned in a response or a log an untrusted party can reach — even when the underlying failure is otherwise handled correctly. Weight lightly, and do not conflate with the above, hardening nits with no plausible attack path: a validated/internal/numeric id used in a path, environment variables passed into a trusted subprocess with no attacker-controlled content, or a missing redundant defense-in-depth layer where the primary control already holds. Do NOT lower the score for framework-mediated safety that is clearly in force: parameterized or ORM-built queries, inputs already validated or type-narrowed at a trust boundary, auth/escaping middleware that is actually applied on the reachable path, and code reachable only by trusted internal callers with no untrusted entry point. Higher means safer against real, reachable attacks.
criteria: A reachable, exploitable critical vulnerability is present: e.g. authentication or access control that fails open, command injection via unsanitized subprocess arguments, path traversal from an unsanitized id/name joined into a filesystem path, or a broken/predictable cryptographic primitive protecting something sensitive (passwords, session tokens)

A serious weakness is present and plausibly reachable by an untrusted caller, even if exploitation needs specific conditions, including an error path that leaks internal detail (stack trace, path, secret) to an untrusted caller
A real but harder-to-reach concern, or a risky pattern whose exploitability is genuinely unclear and needs human review

Only defense-in-depth nits remain: patterns that look risky in isolation (e.g. env vars passed to a trusted subprocess, an id used in a path) but have no plausible attack path because the value is validated, internal, or not attacker-controlled

No apparent security issues; attacker-reachable input is validated or sanitized before use, auth fails closed, no secrets, safe APIs and cryptographic primitives used, and errors do not leak internal detail to untrusted callers

complexity_clean_code.instructions: Rate this source code for complexity and Robert C. Martin clean-code qualities: function size and single responsibility, name clarity, and complexity as a reader would actually feel it. Judge complexity qualitatively, not by literal branch counting (exact counting is a known weak spot for this model). Prefer a cognitive-complexity lens over a cyclomatic one: nested control flow that forces a reader to hold multiple contexts at once (for example a loop containing a try/catch containing a conditional) is worse than the same number of sequential, early-return guard clauses, even when both have a similar number of branches. Higher means simpler and cleaner.
criteria: Very hard to follow: deeply nested control flow that forces holding multiple contexts at once, huge functions, unclear names
Often complex or poorly named; frequent cognitive overload from nesting or mixed concerns, even where individual branch counts look modest
Moderate complexity; some nesting or nested error handling that could flatten into guard clauses, several functions or names could be simpler
Mostly simple and well named; small focused functions with shallow, mostly linear control flow
Clean and simple: small single-purpose functions, clear names, shallow linear control flow with no nested-context reading burden

comments.instructions: Rate the comment discipline of this source code. Good comments explain non-obvious why (hidden invariants, external constraints, justified lint or type suppressions, public API doc contracts). Bad comments narrate what the code already says, add banners, leave commented-out code, or preach about workarounds instead of fixing them. A lint or type suppression is only 'justified' if the comment names the specific reason it is needed (a specific external constraint or a specific known false positive) — a suppression with no reason, or a vague one such as 'needed' or 'temp fix', counts as undisciplined. Higher means better discipline.
criteria: Pervasive narration, banners, commented-out code, or unjustified lint or type suppressions
Many comments restate the code or justify workarounds rather than fixing them
Mixed: some useful comments alongside several redundant what-comments
Mostly disciplined; only a rare redundant comment
Exemplary: comments explain only non-obvious why; no narration, no dead code; every suppression names its specific reason

testability.instructions: Rate how easily this source code can be unit tested: presence of seams, dependency injection, pure versus side-effecting logic, and avoidance of hidden global state. The single sharpest signal is whether a collaborator — a service, client, repository, or other stateful dependency — is constructed inline inside the function or class under review (a bare `new X()` buried in business logic, with no way for a caller to substitute it) versus received as a parameter or constructor argument (a seam a test can use to inject a fake). Inline construction of a collaborator is a stronger testability smell than almost any other pattern, even when the rest of the function is otherwise pure. First judge the file's role from its path, the state's `role_hint` (if present), and its content: testability is a category error for a fixture, mock/stub, type declaration, or story file — there is no logic to unit test, so score it near the top by default unless it does something that would genuinely make it awkward to use from a test (e.g. a hidden side effect on import). For a test file itself, judge only whether its own helpers/setup are testable, not whether the test needs testing. Apply the full bar only to application/business logic.
criteria: Untestable: hidden dependencies, collaborators constructed inline with no injection seam, global state, side effects fused with logic
Hard to test; would need heavy mocking or refactoring first, including reaching inside the module to replace an inline-constructed collaborator
Testable with some effort; a few seams missing
Mostly testable; clear seams and injectable dependencies
Highly testable: pure functions, injected dependencies, clean seams — or a non-logic file (fixture/mock/type/story) with nothing that would resist being used in a test

error_handling.instructions: Rate this source code for error handling: validation at boundaries, meaningful error propagation, and absence of swallowed or ignored failures. Also flag error handling that leaks internal detail to an untrusted caller through the error itself — a stack trace, file path, internal identifier, or secret returned in a response or written to a log an untrusted party can reach — even if the failure is otherwise handled; treat this as a boundary-validation gap, not only a robustness gap (it is also weighted under `security`, so it is fine to flag it in both). First judge the file's role from its path, the state's `role_hint` (if present), and its content: a fixture, mock/stub, type declaration, story, or test file has no boundary to validate and no failure path of its own, so score it near the top by default rather than penalizing it for lacking try/catch or input validation it was never meant to have. Apply the full bar only to code that actually receives external or caller input — application/business logic, request handlers, parsers, and the like. Higher means more robust.
criteria: Failure paths ignored or swallowed; no boundary validation; crashes on bad input, or errors returned to an untrusted caller leak internal detail (stack trace, path, secret)
Weak: broad catches, silent failures, little validation
Partial: some paths handled but gaps remain at boundaries
Mostly robust; only minor gaps

Robust: validates at boundaries, propagates meaningful errors without leaking internal detail, no swallowed exceptions — or a non-logic file (fixture/mock/type/story/test) with no boundary of its own to guard

concurrency_and_idempotency.instructions: Rate this source code for event-loop discipline and idempotency under retries and partial failure. A background loop, periodic poll, reconcile pass, boot sweep, or fill job that iterates a collection whose size grows with the database or workload MUST chunk its synchronous work and yield the event loop between chunks (e.g. via a yield helper) — a tight synchronous loop over an unbounded or growing collection on the shared Node event loop is a critical violation, since it can freeze every other request the process serves. Commands, lifecycle steps, and processing loops must also be idempotent: they should converge to the same end state whether run once or replayed after a crash, restart, or retry, with no double-application of a side effect (e.g. double-charging, double-inserting, re-sending a notification) on a retried attempt. A retry loop or subprocess-spawn loop with no upper bound is also a smell here. First judge the file's role from its path, the state's `role_hint` (if present), and its content: MOST files have no background loop, no shared-state mutation, and no retryable command — pure functions, types, UI components, tests, fixtures, mocks, stories, and config have no such surface at all. Score these near the top (4) by default; do not penalize a file for lacking yield points or idempotency guards it was never meant to have. Apply the full bar only to code that actually runs a loop over a growing collection, a periodic or background job, or a retryable command or lifecycle step.
criteria: Has a background loop, poll, reconcile pass, or retry/spawn loop that is a critical risk: a tight synchronous loop over an unbounded/growing collection with no yield, or a side effect that clearly double-applies on retry
Same surface present but only partially mitigated: yields are missing on some paths, or idempotency holds for the common case but breaks under a plausible crash or retry
Has the surface and mostly handles it correctly, but a genuine gap remains (e.g. an unbounded retry with no cap, or a lifecycle step whose idempotency is unclear)
Has the surface and handles it correctly; only a minor, defensible gap remains
No background loop, retryable command, or shared-state mutation to worry about — or, where present, it chunks/yields correctly and converges to the same end state under crash, restart, or retry

ai_slop.instructions: Rate this source code for tells that it was produced by an LLM coding agent without a human editing pass — a distinct axis from the other categories, which judge whether the code is good; this one judges whether it reads like nobody looked at it twice. Weight, in roughly this order of severity: (1) hallucinated or non-existent imports, packages, or API calls that would fail at build or runtime — the single most damning tell; (2) leftover assistant chatter or meta-commentary embedded in the file itself, e.g. 'As an AI...', 'Here is the updated function', 'I've refactored this to...', apologetic hedges ('this is a simplified version', 'note that this may not be perfect'), or a first-person voice narrating the change rather than describing the code; (3) proliferation of near-identical, differently-named helpers doing the same job (e.g. formatCurrency/formatMoney/displayPrice) instead of reusing or extending one — a machine-scale variant of copy-paste; (4) needless speculative abstraction added with no second caller or driving requirement — an interface, strategy, or config knob behind a single implementation, justified only as 'for future use' or 'for flexibility'; (5) reflexive, blanket defensiveness: a try/catch wrapped around an operation that cannot throw, or the same null/array-length guard repeated verbatim many times instead of validated once at a boundary; (6) generic placeholder naming and unfinished stubs left as if forgotten — data/result/temp/foo/item1, or a TODO/FIXME describing work the surrounding code claims is already done; (7) tutorial-density comments narrating nearly every line at a rate no working human engineer would bother with, even where an individual comment might pass a why-vs-what test in isolation — this can overlap with `comments`; flag it in both when it does, the same way an error that leaks internal detail is flagged under both `security` and `error_handling`. First judge the file's role from its path, the state's `role_hint` (if present), and its content: a generated file, fixture, mock, type declaration, or plain data file has no authorial voice to judge, so score it near the top by default. Higher means the code reads like a deliberate human wrote and edited it, with no AI-agent tells.
criteria: Riddled with AI-agent tells: hallucinated imports or APIs, leftover assistant chatter or apologetic commentary, or several other tells stacked together
Frequent tells a careful human editing pass would have caught: renamed-duplicate helpers, speculative single-implementation abstractions, or blanket defensive wrapping throughout
Some tells present but localized: an isolated placeholder name, one over-defensive block, or one narrated stretch of comments
Mostly clean; only a minor, easy-to-miss tell remains (e.g. one slightly generic name or a single redundant guard)
No AI-agent tells: naming, abstraction, and defensiveness all look deliberate and proportionate to the problem — or a non-authorial file (generated/fixture/mock/type/data) with no voice to judge
